conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I’m so glad you came in today; the first weeks and months with a new baby can bring every emotion at once, and it’s my job to make sure you don’t have to navigate them alone.  

I’d like to do a quick, 10-question screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It helps us understand how mood, anxiety, and stress have been showing up for you over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share here stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification any time.  

When you’re ready, we’ll jump right in.  

To start: Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been as much as always, not quite as much, definitely not as much, or not at all?
I’ve laughed a little, but it’s definitely not as much as before the baby. Things that used to crack me up barely get a smile now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Definitely not as much. I might chuckle if something’s really obvious, but most of the time it feels forced—like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not very often. I still get a tiny spark when I think about grabbing coffee with my best friend next week, but most days it feels like I’m just dragging myself from one feeding to the next.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more often than I’d like to admit. If the baby fusses for a long stretch, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong as a mom.” It’s like a reflex—I know it’s probably not fair, but the guilty thought pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. Even when everything looks fine—baby’s sleeping, no fever, house quiet—I’ll suddenly feel this knot in my chest thinking something bad’s about to happen. I’ll check the monitor three or four times just to be sure, but the worry doesn’t really go away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, sometimes I’ll be rocking the baby in the middle of the night and out of nowhere my heart starts racing, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah... a lot of the time. Some days it feels like the second I finish one thing, two more pop up, and I can’t ever get ahead. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles or the laundry mountain and just feel this wave of “I can’t do this.” I still manage, but it’s like wading through thick mud.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes, that’s been happening. I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I fasten the swaddle tight enough, what if she spits up while I’m asleep, am I already failing her? It takes me forever to drift off, and then I jolt awake at least once or twice with the same worries.
I have felt sad or miserable
Quite often. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over most of my days. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears pooling for no real reason—just this heavy, sad feeling I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes… I’ve cried once or twice this week. It just hits out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding her tiny onesies and suddenly feel so overwhelmed and sad that the tears start before I can stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind once or twice when everything felt like too much. Nothing planned—I’d never leave my baby—but the thought flashed in for a second, like “what if I just weren’t here?” Then I feel awful for even thinking it.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  

Date: ———-  

1. Primary endorsed symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Marked loss of enjoyment / inability to look forward to activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding parenting (Q3)  
- Free-floating anxiety, nocturnal panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, “can’t do this” cognitions (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just weren’t here”) without intent or plan (Q10)  

2. Pattern  
All items cluster in the moderate–severe range; symptoms present most days and interfere with daily functioning and infant care.  

3. Screening significance  
Score pattern consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features in the postpartum period. Passive suicidal ideation elevates acute risk.  

4. Risk factors highlighted  
- Depressed mood + anhedonia (core mood indicators)  
- Anxiety/panic attacks (possible postpartum anxiety disorder)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination, not solely infant demands  
- Excessive maternal guilt / cognitive distortions  
- Self-harm cognitions → safety concern  

5. Next steps for referral  
Recommend immediate formal psychiatric evaluation (within 24–48 h) to confirm diagnosis, assess safety, and develop management plan. Provide crisis resources and ensure accompanying adult is aware of emergency protocols.
